concepts.title: FLP Impossibility Theorem
concepts.content: Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson proved no deterministic consensus protocol guarantees both safety and liveness in an asynchronous network if even one process can fail by crashing (`f = 1`). Practical systems like Raft and Paxos preserve safety unconditionally and circumvent FLP using randomized election timeouts or partial synchrony (`--election-timeout` in etcd).
concepts.image_prompt: Triangle trade-off diagram showing nodes Safety, Liveness, and Asynchronous Crash Resilience with arrows pointing to a central node labeled Deterministic Consensus Impossible, and a bypass branch labeled Randomized Timeout.

concepts.title: CAP Theorem vs PACELC
concepts.content: During a network partition (`P`), a distributed data store must choose between linearizable consistency (`C`) and 100% availability (`A`). PACELC extends this: even without partitions (`E`), systems trade latency (`L`) against consistency (`C`). For example, DynamoDB is PA/EL with eventual reads, while Spanner and etcd operate as PC/EC.
concepts.image_prompt: Decision tree diagram starting at node Partition P, branching Yes to Consistency C vs Availability A, and branching No to Else E leading to Latency L vs Consistency C.

concepts.title: Network Partitions and Asymmetric Links
concepts.content: Network partitions isolate node subsets or create asymmetric links where Node A reaches Node B, but B cannot reach A, or C reaches both. Asymmetric drops cause disruptive leadership churn in naive Raft setups unless `PreVote` is enabled (`ETCD_ENABLE_PPROF` / Raft `PreVote=true`) to verify quorum reachability before incrementing terms.
concepts.image_prompt: Network topology diagram with three nodes A, B, and C, showing a solid bidirectional arrow between A and C, a unidirectional arrow from A to B, and a blocked arrow from B to C.

concepts.title: Lamport Logical Clocks
concepts.content: Lamport clocks establish a partial causal ordering of events without synchronized physical clocks. Each process maintains a counter `L`, incrementing `L = L + 1` before local events and setting `L = max(L_local, L_msg) + 1` on message receipt. If event `a -> b`, then `L(a) < L(b)`, though `L(a) < L(b)` does not imply causality.
concepts.image_prompt: Space-time sequence diagram with processes P1 and P2 showing horizontal timelines, local counter increments L=1 to L=2, and a diagonal message arrow updating receiver counter via max(L_local, L_msg)+1.

concepts.title: Vector Clocks and Causality Detection
concepts.content: Vector clocks track exact causal history across `N` nodes using an array `V[1..N]`. Unlike Lamport timestamps, vector clocks detect concurrent conflicting writes: two versions `V1` and `V2` are concurrent (`V1 || V2`) when neither `V1[i] <= V2[i]` for all `i` nor the reverse holds. Amazon Dynamo uses this to surface sibling values.
concepts.image_prompt: Directed acyclic version graph showing nodes A, B, and C with 3-element vector arrays [1,0,0], concurrent branches [1,1,0] and [1,0,1], converging into a conflict resolution merge node [2,1,1].

concepts.title: Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC)
concepts.content: Hybrid Logical Clocks combine physical NTP wall time (`pt`) with a logical counter (`l`, typically 16 bits) into a monotonic tuple `(l_wall, l_logical)`. Used by CockroachDB and MongoDB, HLC provides bounded causal timestamps close to physical time without TrueTime hardware, failing safe if NTP drift stays below `--max-offset` (default `500ms` in CockroachDB).
concepts.image_prompt: Block diagram of a 64-bit timestamp split into 48-bit Physical Time component fed by NTP Clock and 16-bit Logical Counter incremented on same-millisecond causal events.

concepts.title: TrueTime and Bounded Clock Uncertainty
concepts.content: Google Spanner's TrueTime API exposes physical time as an uncertainty interval `[earliest, latest]` where `epsilon = (latest - earliest) / 2` (typically `1ms` to `7ms`) using GPS receivers and atomic clocks. To guarantee external consistency across shards without cross-shard communication, Spanner waits `2 * epsilon` (commit wait) before releasing locks.
concepts.image_prompt: Timeline diagram showing Transaction T1 commit wait spanning interval [t_earliest, t_latest] of width 2 epsilon before Transaction T2 starts, with GPS and Atomic Clock inputs feeding the uncertainty bound.

concepts.title: Linearizability (Strong Consistency)
concepts.content: Linearizability is a single-object, real-time guarantee: every operation appears to take effect atomically at a single point between its invocation and completion, and all clients observe a consistent state order. In etcd or ZooKeeper, linearizable reads require quorum confirmation or valid leader leases (`etcdctl get key --consistency=l`).
concepts.image_prompt: Client execution timeline showing overlapping Read and Write invocation bars across Client A and Client B, with vertical linearization points ordering operations strictly within their start and end bounds.

concepts.title: Sequential vs Causal Consistency
concepts.content: Sequential consistency removes real-time bounds: operations appear in a single total order across all nodes that respects each client's program order. Causal consistency is weaker and available during partitions (`CA` under PACELC), ordering only causally related operations (`a -> b`) while allowing concurrent writes to be observed in different orders.
concepts.image_prompt: Two-panel sequence diagram comparing Sequential Consistency with a single global serialized queue versus Causal Consistency showing causal arrows ordered identically and concurrent writes reordered across replicas.

concepts.title: Read-Your-Writes and Monotonic Reads
concepts.content: Session guarantees prevent jarring anomalies in eventually consistent or follower-read systems. Read-Your-Writes ensures a client always sees its own prior updates, while Monotonic Reads guarantees a client never observes an older state after seeing a newer one. Implement both by pinning clients to replica LSNs (`min_lsn >= client_high_water_mark`).
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence diagram showing Client writing LSN=15 to Leader, then sending a Read request with metadata min_lsn=15 to a Follower, which waits until replication reaches LSN=15 before replying.

concepts.title: Strict Quorum Intersection (R + W > N)
concepts.content: In leaderless replication (Cassandra, Dynamo), configuring write quorum `W` and read quorum `R` across `N` replicas such that `R + W > N` guarantees at least one overlapping node holds the latest timestamped write. A common production fault-tolerant setup uses `N = 3, W = 2, R = 2` (`LOCAL_QUORUM`), tolerating `1` replica failure.
concepts.image_prompt: Venn diagram of N=3 replica nodes (Node 1, Node 2, Node 3) showing Write Set W=2 overlapping with Read Set R=2 at central intersection Node 2.

concepts.title: Sloppy Quorums and Hinted Handoff
concepts.content: When network partitions prevent reaching `W` designated home nodes on a consistent hash ring, sloppy quorums maintain write availability by writing to temporary fallback nodes (`hinted handoff`). While `W` acknowledgments still succeed, `R + W > N` no longer guarantees linearizable reads until hints replay after partition recovery (`nodetool statushandoff`).
concepts.image_prompt: Consistent hash ring diagram with replicas A, B, and unreachable node C, showing Coordinator writing a hinted handoff copy to neighbor node D and replaying to C upon recovery.

concepts.title: Anti-Entropy with Merkle Trees
concepts.content: Leaderless databases repair silent replica divergence in the background using Merkle trees—hierarchical cryptographic hash trees over key ranges. Replicas exchange root hashes first and recursively traverse only mismatched branches in `O(log K)` steps rather than transferring entire datasets. In Cassandra, trigger synchronization carefully via `nodetool repair -pr`.
concepts.image_prompt: Binary hash tree comparison diagram between Replica 1 and Replica 2 showing matching left subtree hashes and highlighted diverging path from Root Hash down to Leaf Key Range [K50..K75].

concepts.title: Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs)
concepts.content: CRDTs enable multi-master concurrent updates without coordination by guaranteeing strong eventual convergence. State-based CRDTs (`CvRDTs`) form a join-semilattice where merge (`⊔`) is commutative, associative, and idempotent (e.g., PN-Counter using separate increment `P` and decrement `N` vectors). Watch out for metadata bloat from tombstones in Observed-Remove Sets (`OR-Set`).
concepts.image_prompt: Join-semilattice diagram showing Replica A and Replica B independently incrementing state vectors P and N, then exchanging states via a commutative, idempotent Merge operator to reach identical state.

concepts.title: Single-Decree Synod Paxos
concepts.content: Classic Paxos reaches consensus on a single value across Proposers, Acceptors, and Learners in two phases. In Phase 1a/1b (`Prepare`/`Promise`), a proposer picks unique ballot `n` and gathers quorum promises to reject ballots `< n` while learning the highest-numbered accepted value `(v_max, n_max)`. Phase 2a/2b (`Accept`/`Accepted`) proposes `v_max` (or its own value if none).
concepts.image_prompt: Two-phase message sequence diagram between Proposer and three Acceptors showing Phase 1 Prepare(n) and Promise(n, v_max) followed by Phase 2 Accept(n, v) and quorum Accepted acks.

concepts.title: Multi-Paxos and Leader Lease Optimization
concepts.content: Running two-phase Synod Paxos per log slot requires `2` network round-trips (`2 RTTs`). Multi-Paxos elects a stable distinguished leader via a single Phase 1 `Prepare` across all future instances (`index >= i`), reducing steady-state log replication to Phase 2 (`Accept`/`Accepted`) in `1 RTT`. Dueling proposers are prevented via leader heartbeats or leases.
concepts.image_prompt: Timeline comparison diagram showing Basic Paxos repeating Phase 1 and Phase 2 per slot versus Multi-Paxos executing Phase 1 once for leadership followed by pipelined 1-RTT Phase 2 slots.

concepts.title: Raft Consensus Overview and Term Numbers
concepts.content: Raft decomposes state machine replication into Leader Election, Log Replication, and Safety. Every node is in one of three states (`Follower`, `Candidate`, `Leader`), and time is divided into monotonically increasing `term` numbers acting as a logical clock. Any RPC carrying a higher `term` immediately forces the receiver to step down to `Follower`.
concepts.image_prompt: Finite state machine diagram with nodes Follower, Candidate, and Leader connected by transition arrows labeled Election Timeout, Receives Majority Votes, and Discovers Higher Term.

concepts.title: Raft Leader Election and Split Votes
concepts.content: When a Follower receives no `AppendEntries` heartbeat within its randomized election timeout (commonly `150ms–300ms`), it increments `currentTerm`, transitions to `Candidate`, votes for itself, and broadcasts `RequestVote` RPCs. Randomized timeouts prevent perpetual split-vote livelocks; each server grants at most one vote per term (`votedFor`) on a first-come, up-to-date basis.
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence diagram showing Follower A timing out at 165ms before Follower B at 280ms, incrementing Term T+1, sending RequestVote RPCs, and collecting majority votes to become Leader.

concepts.title: Raft Log Replication and Commit Index
concepts.content: A Raft leader appends client commands to its local log as `(term, index, command)` and sends `AppendEntries` RPCs to followers in parallel. Once a majority (`floor(N/2) + 1`) appends the entry, the leader advances `commitIndex`, applies the entry to its deterministic state machine, replies to the client, and notifies followers of `leaderCommit` in subsequent heartbeats.
concepts.image_prompt: Log array diagram across Leader and two Followers showing indexed slots with Term numbers, replication arrows for slot 5, majority ack updating commitIndex=5, and state machine execution.

concepts.title: Raft Election Safety Restriction
concepts.content: Unlike systems that ship missing log entries to a newly elected leader, Raft enforces unidirectional log flow from leader to followers. A voter denies `RequestVote` if the candidate's log is less up-to-date than its own—compared first by `lastLogTerm`, then by `lastLogIndex` (`candidateTerm > myTerm || (candidateTerm == myTerm && candidateIdx >= myIdx)`).
concepts.image_prompt: Flowchart inside a Voter node evaluating RequestVote(lastLogTerm, lastLogIndex) against local log tail, branching to Grant Vote only if Candidate Term is higher or equal with longer Index.

concepts.title: Raft Commit Rule for Prior Terms
concepts.content: Section 5.4.2 of the Raft paper proves a subtle safety hazard: a leader must never commit log entries from a previous term purely by counting replicas, because a future leader could still overwrite them. A new leader commits prior-term entries indirectly only by replicating and committing at least one entry from its `currentTerm` (often an immediate `no-op` entry on election).
concepts.image_prompt: Multi-node log grid showing Leader in Term 4 appending a Term 4 no-op entry after uncommitted Term 2 entries, locking and committing both only after majority replication of Term 4.

concepts.title: Raft Linearizable Reads: ReadIndex and LeaseRead
concepts.content: Serving reads directly from a Raft leader's memory risks returning stale data if the leader was silently partitioned and superseded. `ReadIndex` records `commitIndex` and sends a lightweight quorum heartbeat round to confirm leadership before reading (`1 RTT`, zero disk I/O). `LeaseRead` uses bounded clock drift to skip the heartbeat, trading clock-skew risk for local speed.
concepts.image_prompt: Two-path flow diagram comparing ReadIndex recording commitIndex and confirming majority Heartbeat ACK before state read versus LeaseRead checking local clock bound before immediate state read.

concepts.title: Raft Membership Changes: Joint Consensus vs Single-Server
concepts.content: Switching cluster membership directly from `C_old` to `C_new` risks two disjoint majorities electing concurrent leaders during the transition. Joint consensus commits an intermediate configuration `C_old,new` requiring separate majorities from both sets. Modern implementations (etcd, HashiCorp Raft) prefer single-server changes, adding or removing one node at a time so old and new majorities always overlap.
concepts.image_prompt: Cluster overlap diagram contrasting unsafe direct jump from 3-node C_old to 5-node C_new with disjoint majorities versus safe single-node step C_old (3) to C_new (4) with intersecting quorums.

concepts.title: Raft Log Compaction and InstallSnapshot
concepts.content: Unbounded Raft logs exhaust disk space and slow node recovery. Periodically, each node snapshots its current state machine alongside `(lastIncludedIndex, lastIncludedTerm)` and truncates prior log entries. If a lagging or newly joined follower requires entries already compacted away, the leader streams the snapshot via `InstallSnapshot` RPCs (`--snapshot-count=10000` in etcd).
concepts.image_prompt: Storage block diagram showing Raft Log entries 1..10000 replaced by a single Snapshot block(lastIndex=10000, lastTerm=3) and an InstallSnapshot arrow streaming to a lagging Follower.

concepts.title: Raft PreVote Extension
concepts.content: When a partitioned follower repeatedly times out without `PreVote`, it increments `currentTerm` to a high number; upon rejoining, it forces the healthy leader to step down and disrupts cluster availability. With `PreVote` enabled, a prospective candidate first sends `RequestPreVote` and only increments `currentTerm` if a quorum confirms its log is up-to-date and no valid leader heartbeat exists.
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence diagram showing Partitioned Node sending RequestPreVote(nextTerm) on heal, receiving Reject from Follower with active Leader heartbeat, and rejoining without incrementing currentTerm.

concepts.title: Flexible Paxos Quorum Intersection
concepts.content: Howard et al. proved that Paxos does not require all quorums to intersect with each other; safety only requires that every Phase 1 (leader election) quorum `Q1` intersects with every Phase 2 (replication) quorum `Q2` (`Q1 + Q2 > N`). In a `10`-node cluster, setting `Q2 = 3` and `Q1 = 8` lowers steady-state replication latency while penalizing rare leader elections.
concepts.image_prompt: Grid of N=10 nodes showing a small 3-node Phase 2 replication quorum intersecting at one node with an 8-node Phase 1 election quorum.

concepts.title: Viewstamped Replication (VR) and Zab
concepts.content: Viewstamped Replication (1988) pioneered primary-backup replication using view numbers (`v`) and view-change protocols decades before Raft. Apache ZooKeeper's Zab (`ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast`) uses a similar epoch-based two-phase commit (`zxid = (epoch << 32) | counter`) with FIFO TCP channels, enforcing total prefix ordering so every state update applies in strict causal sequence.
concepts.image_prompt: 64-bit ZXID structure diagram split into 32-bit Epoch and 32-bit Counter, feeding a FIFO TCP broadcast pipeline from Leader to Followers with two-phase Proposal and Commit steps.

concepts.title: Byzantine Fault Tolerance and 3f + 1 Bound
concepts.content: Crash-fault protocols (`Raft`, `Paxos`) require `2f + 1` nodes to tolerate `f` non-malicious crashes. When nodes can suffer arbitrary corruption, lie, or collude (Byzantine faults), consensus requires at least `N >= 3f + 1` nodes. Out of `N` nodes, `f` may be unreachable, so `N - f` must respond, and among those responses, honest nodes must outnumber `f` liars (`N - 2f > f`).
concepts.image_prompt: Quorum breakdown diagram of N=3f+1 nodes showing f unresponsive nodes, f malicious lying nodes, and f+1 honest nodes forming a strict majority among the 2f+1 responses.

concepts.title: PBFT (Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance)
concepts.content: Castro and Liskov's PBFT achieves Byzantine consensus in partially synchronous networks using `3f + 1` replicas across three phases: `Pre-Prepare` (Primary assigns sequence number `n`), `Prepare` (all-to-all broadcast waiting for `2f` matching messages), and `Commit` (all-to-all broadcast waiting for `2f + 1` commits). Its `O(N^2)` message complexity limits classic PBFT to small validator sets.
concepts.image_prompt: All-to-all message sequence diagram across Primary and three Replicas (including one faulty node) showing Client Request, Pre-Prepare, all-to-all Prepare mesh, and all-to-all Commit mesh.

concepts.title: Two-Phase Commit (2PC) and Coordinator Blocking
concepts.content: Two-Phase Commit ensures atomic distributed transactions across shards via a `Prepare` voting phase and a `Commit`/`Abort` phase, logging durability states via Write-Ahead Logging (`WAL`). Its fatal flaw is blocking: if a participant votes `YES` (`Prepared`) and both the Coordinator and another participant crash, surviving nodes must hold locks indefinitely until the coordinator recovers.
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence diagram of Coordinator and two Shards showing Phase 1 Prepare/Vote Yes with WAL write, followed by Coordinator Crash leaving Shard 1 blocked holding locks in Uncertain state.

concepts.title: Saga Pattern and Compensating Transactions
concepts.content: Sagas avoid long-lived distributed locks across microservices by decomposing a workflow into local acid transactions `T_1, T_2, ..., T_n` paired with semantic undo actions `C_1, C_2, ..., C_{n-1}`. On failure at `T_k`, the orchestrator executes compensations in reverse order. Because Sagas lack `ACID` isolation (`ACD` only), counter measures like semantic locks and idempotency keys are mandatory.
concepts.image_prompt: Workflow sequence diagram showing forward transactions T1 (Order), T2 (Reserve), and failing T3 (Charge), triggering reverse compensating path C2 (Release) and C1 (Cancel).

concepts.title: Calvin vs Spanner Distributed Transactions
concepts.content: Spanner executes distributed transactions using dynamic two-phase locking (`2PL`) over Paxos groups and TrueTime commit wait. Calvin eliminates distributed commit protocols (`2PC`) and lock contention pauses by using a consensus layer to agree on a deterministic transaction batch order up front; replicas then execute the identical deterministic schedule independently without coordination.
concepts.image_prompt: Side-by-side architecture diagram comparing Spanner executing 2PL plus 2PC across Paxos shards during runtime versus Calvin ordering inputs in a Sequencer Log before lock-free deterministic execution.

concepts.title: Phi Accrual Failure Detector
concepts.content: Instead of outputting a boolean `up/down` decision from a fixed heartbeat timeout, Hayashibara's Phi Accrual Failure Detector (used in Cassandra and Akka) models inter-arrival times as a normal distribution and outputs a continuous suspicion level `phi = -log10(P_later(t_now - t_last))`. In Cassandra, `phi_convict_threshold: 8` corresponds to a `10^-8` probability that the node is merely delayed.
concepts.image_prompt: Probability curve diagram showing heartbeat inter-arrival distribution feeding a calculation block for phi suspicion score, crossing threshold phi=8 to trigger Node Down action.

concepts.title: SWIM Gossip Protocol and Lifeguard
concepts.content: Traditional all-to-all heartbeats scale poorly at `O(N^2)`. SWIM (`Scalable Weakly-consistent Infection-style Process Group Membership`) separates failure detection from membership dissemination using `O(1)` periodic direct `ping` probes, fallback indirect `ping-req(k)` probes through `k` peers, and piggybacked gossip updates. HashiCorp Consul's Lifeguard adds dynamic self-awareness (`LHA`) to suppress false positives under CPU saturation.
concepts.image_prompt: Network diagram showing Node A sending a failed direct Ping to Node B, then sending Indirect Ping-Req through peers C and D, which successfully probe B and return Ack.

concepts.title: Fencing Tokens and Split-Brain Prevention
concepts.content: Distributed locks leased via Redis (`Redlock`) or ZooKeeper can expire during a client's stop-the-world GC pause, allowing a second client to acquire the lock while the first still believes it holds leadership. To prevent split-brain corruption, the lock service issues a monotonically increasing `fencing_token` (e.g., ZooKeeper `zxid` or etcd `ModRevision`), and storage rejects writes with `token < max_seen_token`.
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence diagram showing Client 1 acquiring Lock(token=33), pausing for GC while Client 2 acquires Lock(token=34) and writes to Storage, followed by Storage rejecting Client 1's delayed write(token=33).

concepts.title: Chubby and ZooKeeper Ephemeral Sequential Nodes
concepts.content: ZooKeeper coordinates distributed locks and leader election without polling storms (`herd effect`) by combining `EPHEMERAL_SEQUENTIAL` znodes with watches. Each contender creates `/election/n_` and receives a monotonic suffix (e.g., `n_0002`); if it does not hold the lowest number, it sets a `getData` watch solely on the immediately preceding node (`n_0001`) rather than the root.
concepts.image_prompt: Ordered chain diagram of ZooKeeper ephemeral znodes n_0001 (Leader), n_0002, and n_0003, showing Watch pointers directed exclusively from n_0003 to n_0002 and from n_0002 to n_0001.

concepts.title: Chain Replication and CRAQ
concepts.content: Chain Replication organizes replicas linearly (`Head -> Middle -> Tail`): all writes enter the `Head` and propagate sequentially down the chain, while all linearizable reads are served exclusively by the `Tail`. CRAQ (`Chain Replication with Apportioned Queries`) scales read throughput across all nodes by letting intermediate replicas serve `clean` committed versions directly or query the `Tail` when a key is `dirty`.
concepts.image_prompt: Linear chain diagram with Head, Middle, and Tail nodes showing Writes propagating left-to-right, Tail marking versions Clean, and Clients reading Clean keys from Middle or querying Tail on Dirty.

concepts.title: Consistent Hashing with Bounded Loads
concepts.content: Consistent hashing maps both nodes and keys onto a `2^32` or `2^64` hash ring using `v` virtual nodes per physical server so adding or removing a node remaps only `O(K/N)` keys. To prevent hot keys from overloading a single shard, Consistent Hashing with Bounded Loads caps each node's capacity at `ceil(c * average_load)` (e.g., `c = 1.25`), spilling excess requests clockwise.
concepts.image_prompt: Circular hash ring showing Virtual Nodes and Key requests, where overloaded Node A reaches capacity factor c=1.25 and forwards overflow key K99 clockwise to successor Node B.

concepts.title: etcd MVCC Compaction and Defragmentation
concepts.content: etcd stores every key modification as an immutable revision in a BoltDB (`bbolt`) B+tree to support Kubernetes resourceVersion watches. When the database hits `--quota-backend-bytes` (default `2 GiB`, max recommended `8 GiB`), etcd raises a `NOSPACE` alarm and rejects writes. Recover by compacting old revisions (`etcdctl compact $REV`), defragmenting per member (`etcdctl defrag`), and disarming (`etcdctl alarm disarm`).
concepts.image_prompt: Three-step operational pipeline showing BoltDB filled with old MVCC revisions, Step 1 Compact marking revisions free, Step 2 Defrag reclaiming disk space, and Step 3 Alarm Disarm restoring writes.

concepts.title: Jepsen Testing and Nemesis Fault Injection
concepts.content: Kyle Kingsbury's Jepsen framework validates distributed systems by running concurrent client operations against a cluster while a `Nemesis` injects faults (asymmetric network partitions via `iptables`, `SIGSTOP` process pauses, and `libfaketime` clock skew). Jepsen records the concurrent invocation/completion history `.edn` file and verifies safety invariants using Knossos (linearizability) or Elle (transactional cycle detection).
concepts.image_prompt: System test architecture showing Jepsen Clients and Nemesis fault injector interacting with a 5-node cluster, outputting an execution history log to Elle and Knossos consistency checkers.
